captions.text: In 1989, the Sun helped shut down an entire power grid.
Millions of people in Quebec lost electricity for nine hours.
It was a cloud of magnetized plasma thrown into space by the Sun: a coronal mass ejection.
When it reached Earth, it disturbed our planet's magnetic field.
That changing field drove electric currents through the ground and long power lines.
Protective equipment tripped, and Quebec's grid collapsed.
The same storm also produced auroras far from the poles.
In 1859, the Carrington storm disrupted telegraph systems, and some operators reported sparks.
Today, satellites monitor the Sun, and grid operators can prepare.
But forecasting exactly how a storm will affect infrastructure remains difficult.
Not every solar storm causes a blackout.
The danger depends on the storm, Earth's magnetic response, and the grid itself.
The lights in the sky are beautiful. They are also a reminder:
Our technology lives inside space weather. Save this and subscribe for more real science.
